concepts.title: encoder
concepts.one_liner: The encoder transforms the input image into a representation composed of coefficients and a low pass residual.
concepts.content:
This architecture has two parts: (1) the analysis network (or encoder) that transforms the input image $\mathbf{x}$ into a representation composed of $\mathbf{l}_0, \mathbf{l}_1, ...$ and the low pass residual $\mathbf{x}_n$; and (2) the synthesis network (or decoder) that reconstructs the input from the representation. The Laplacian pyramid is an overcomplete representation (more coefficients than pixels); the dimensionality of the representation is higher than the dimensionality of the input.

Encoder and decoder networks are also common building blocks of deep neural networks. The Laplacian pyramid can be considered as a special type of deep neural net.
concepts.motivation_md: Encoders transform images into representations that capture essential features for reconstruction and analysis, enabling effective image processing and neural network design.
concepts.recap_md:
- The encoder is the analysis network transforming input images into a representation.
- It produces coefficients $\mathbf{l}_0, \mathbf{l}_1, ...$ and a low pass residual $\mathbf{x}_n$.
- The Laplacian pyramid representation is overcomplete, with higher dimensionality than the input.

concepts.title: image blending algorithm using Laplacian pyramid
aliases: image blending algorithm using Laplacian pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The Laplacian pyramid image blending algorithm achieves smooth transitions between images by blending across multiple spatial scales.
concepts.content:
Adelson @Burt83 introduced an image blending algorithm using Laplacian pyramid capable of achieve a smooth transition between the two images. This approach remains one of the best solutions to this problem.

Using the Laplacian pyramid, we can transition from one image to the next over many different spatial scales to make a gradual transition between the two images. The algorithm proceeds as follows. We first build the Laplacian pyramid for the two input images; in this example we use seven levels and we also keep the last low-pass residual as shown in @fig-blending_pyrs.

(see figure: Laplacian pyramids (seven levels and Gaussian residual) for both input images.)

The second step is to build the Gaussian pyramid of the mask as shown in @fig-blending_pyrs_mask (note that we use eight levels, one level more than for the Laplacian pyramid).

(see figure: Gaussian pyramid of the mask.)



In the third step, we combine the three pyramids to compute the Laplacian pyramid of the blended image. The Laplacian pyramid of the blended image is obtained as
$$\mathbf{l}_k = \mathbf{l}_k^A * \mathbf{m}_k + \mathbf{l}_i^B * (1-\mathbf{m}_k)$$
The same is done for the low-pass residual.

Finally, the fourth step consists in collapsing (i.e., decoding) the resulting pyramid to produce the blended image shown in @fig-appleorange.

(see figure: Image compositing with the Laplacian pyramid. Example inspired by @{Burt83}.)

The result in @fig-appleorange has a smooth transition between the two sides and produces a pleasing blending. The mask does no need to be rectangular. It is possible to blend arbitrary images with complex masks, but the quality of the final image will depend on how well aligned the images are and the composition of the objects in the scene. This is method remains one of the most popular methods for image blending due to its simplicity and the quality of the resulting images.
concepts.motivation_md: This algorithm solves the challenge of creating smooth, seamless transitions between images by blending across multiple spatial scales using Laplacian and Gaussian pyramids.
concepts.recap_md:
- The algorithm builds Laplacian pyramids for input images and a Gaussian pyramid for the mask.
- It blends images at each pyramid level using the mask coefficients.
- Collapsing the blended pyramid produces a smooth composite image.

concepts.title: steerable pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The steerable pyramid is a multiscale oriented representation that adds information about image orientation.
concepts.content: The steerable pyramid adds information about image orientation. Therefore, the steerable representation is a multiscale oriented representation that is translation-invariant. It is non-aliased and self-invertible. Ideally, we'd like to have an image transformation that was shiftable, that is, where we could perform interpolations in position, scale, and orientation using linear combinations of a set of basis coefficients.
concepts.motivation_md: The steerable pyramid provides a representation that captures image orientation and scale, enabling flexible image analysis and interpolation.

- Enables shiftable transformations for interpolation in position, scale, and orientation.

concepts.title: Image Pyramids
concepts.one_liner: Image pyramids provide an efficient representation for space-scale invariant processing by representing images at multiple resolutions and scales.
concepts.content:
In @sec-linear_image_filtering we motivated translation invariant linear filters as a way to account for objects appearing at any location in images. Besides translation invariance, scale invariance is fundamental because objects at different distances appear at different sizes, as shown in @fig-birds_multiscale. To locate all bird instances, an operator invariant to translation and scale is needed. Image pyramids provide an efficient representation for space-scale invariant processing.

Image information occurs over many spatial scales. Image pyramids (multiresolution representations) are useful for analyzing and manipulating images across scales. We discuss three types: Gaussian pyramid (multiple resolutions), Laplacian pyramid (breaks image into isotropic spatial frequency bands), and steerable pyramid (separates scales and orientations).

For example, detecting birds of different sizes with a fixed-size template requires multiple templates or a multiscale image pyramid. The pyramid is constructed by scaling down the image by 25% at each level, reducing pixels to 3/4 the size of the previous image. This approach is computationally efficient since convolutions remain small.

Multiscale image processing and pyramids have many applications beyond scale-invariant object detection. This chapter describes important image pyramids and their uses.

(see figure: Objects in images appear at arbitrary locations and with arbitrary image sizes.)

(see figure: Multiscale image pyramid. Each image is 25 percent smaller than the previous one. The red box indicates the size of a template used for detecting birds. As the size of the template is fixed; it will...)
concepts.motivation_md: Objects appear at arbitrary locations and scales in images; image pyramids enable efficient, scale- and translation-invariant processing to detect and analyze such objects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image pyramids represent images at multiple resolutions for multiscale analysis.
- Gaussian, Laplacian, and steerable pyramids offer different frequency and orientation decompositions.
- Multiscale pyramids enable efficient detection of objects at varying sizes.

key_passage.text: Image pyramids (i.e., multiresolution representations for images) are a useful data structure for analyzing and manipulating images over a range of spatial scales.

motivation.text: In addition to translation invariance, scale invariance is another fundamental property of images. Due to perspective projection, objects at different distances will appear with different sizes as shown in fig-birds_multiscale. Therefore, if we want to locate all the bird instances in this image, we will have to apply an operator that is invariant in translation and in scale. Image pyramids provide an efficient representation for space-scale invariant processing.

example.text: As a motivating example, let's assume we want to detect the birds from fig-birds_multiscale. If we have a template of a bird, normalized correlation will be able to detect only the birds that have a similar image size than the template. To introduce scale invariance, one possible solution is to change the size of the template to cover a wide range of possible sizes and apply them to the image. Then, the ensemble of templates will be able to detect birds of different sizes. The disadvantage of this approach is that it will be computationally expensive as detecting large birds will require computing convolutions with big kernels, which is very slow. Another alternative is to change the image size as shown in fig-birds_multiscale_processing, resulting in a multiscale image pyramid. Now we can use the pyramid to detect birds at different sizes using a single template. The red box in the figure denotes the size of the template used. The figure shows how birds of different sizes become detectable at, at least, one of the levels of the pyramid. This method will be more efficient as the template can be kept small and the convolutions will remain computationally efficient.

concepts.title: Linear Image Transforms
concepts.one_liner: A linear image transform represents an image as coefficients via projections onto basis vectors and can be invertible, oversampled, or undersampled.
concepts.content:
For an input image $\boldsymbol\ell$ with $N$ pixels, a linear transform is given by:
$$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol\ell$$
where $\mathbf{r}$ is a vector of dimensionality $M$, and $\mathbf{P}$ is an $N \times M$ matrix. The columns of $\mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, ..., \mathbf{P}_{M-1}]$ are the projection vectors. The transform coefficients are $\mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol\ell$. Thus, $\mathbf{r}$ is a representation of the image $\boldsymbol\ell$ in a different basis than the original pixels.

We want transforms that are invertible, so the input $\boldsymbol\ell$ can be recovered from coefficients $\mathbf{r}$:
$$\boldsymbol\ell = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{r} = \sum_{i=0}^{M-1} \mathbf{r}_i \mathbf{Q}_i$$
where columns of $\mathbf{Q} = [\mathbf{Q}_0, \mathbf{Q}_1, ..., \mathbf{Q}_{M-1}]$ are basis vectors. The input is reconstructed as a linear combination of basis vectors weighted by coefficients.

The transform $\mathbf{P}$ is **critically sampled** if $M=N$, **oversampled** if $M > N$, and **undersampled** if $M < N$. The transform is complete (encodes all image structure) if invertible. If critically sampled and complete, then $\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T})^{-1}$. If overcomplete and complete, the inverse is the pseudoinverse $\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T})^{-1} \mathbf{P}$.

An important special case is when the transform is **self-inverting**, satisfying $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{I}$. The transform values can be real or complex (e.g., Fourier transform). For complex transforms, replace $\mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T}$ by the conjugate transpose.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear image transforms provide alternate representations of images via projections onto basis vectors, enabling invertible, efficient encoding and reconstruction of image data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Linear image transforms represent images as coefficients via projections onto basis vectors.
- Transforms can be critically sampled ($M=N$), oversampled ($M > N$), or undersampled ($M < N$).
- Invertible transforms allow reconstruction of the original image from coefficients.

concepts.title: quadrature mirror filter (QMF) transform
concepts.one_liner: The quadrature mirror filter (QMF) transform is a self-inverting transform equivalent to convolution with orthogonal kernels and has a multiscale version.
concepts.content:
The quadrature mirror filter (QMF) transform is an example of a self-inverting transform @Adelson87b. For 1D signals of length 4, the QMF transform matrix is:
$$
\mathbf{P} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
$$
This corresponds to convolving the input signal with two orthogonal kernels, $[1,1]$ and $[1,-1]$, with stride 2.

This transform also has a multiscale version that is self-inverting.
concepts.motivation_md: The QMF transform provides a self-inverting, efficient way to analyze signals via convolution with orthogonal kernels, useful in multiscale signal processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- The QMF transform is self-inverting and represented by a specific matrix.
- It corresponds to convolution with orthogonal kernels $[1,1]$ and $[1,-1]$ with stride 2.
- A multiscale version of the QMF transform exists and is also self-inverting.

concepts.title: Gaussian Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: A Gaussian pyramid is a recursive multiresolution image representation created by low-pass filtering and downsampling repeatedly.
concepts.content:
A Gaussian pyramid is a recursive algorithm to create multiresolution versions of an image. A Gaussian filter is natural for blurring because successive applications equal a single wider Gaussian filter.

The algorithm involves two steps: convolving the image with a low-pass filter (e.g., the fourth binomial filter $\mathbf{b}_4 = [1,4,6,4,1]/16$, normalized) separably in each dimension, then subsampling by a factor of 2. Each level is obtained by filtering the previous level with the binomial filter and downsampling by 2 in each dimension. Applied recursively, this generates a sequence of images, each smaller and lower resolution than the previous.

@fig-gausspyr shows a Gaussian pyramid with six levels, each half the resolution of the previous. The pyramid is built independently for each color channel.

The two steps can be written in matrix form for a 1D image:
$$\mathbf{g}_{k+1} = \mathbf{D}_k \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{g}_k = \mathbf{G}_k \mathbf{g}_k$$
where $\mathbf{D}_k$ is the downsampling operator, $\mathbf{B}_k$ is convolution with the binomial filter, and $\mathbf{G}_k = \mathbf{D}_k \mathbf{B}_k$ is the blur-and-downsample operator for level $k$.

One block of Gaussian pyramid computation is shown in the diagram.

The sequence $\mathbf{g}_0, \mathbf{g}_1, ..., \mathbf{g}_N$ is called the Gaussian pyramid.

concepts.recap_md:
- Gaussian pyramids recursively blur and downsample images to create multiresolution representations.
- Each level is half the resolution of the previous.
- The process can be expressed as a matrix operation combining blur and downsampling.

concepts.title: Laplacian Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The Laplacian pyramid represents image details lost between Gaussian pyramid levels by subtracting an upsampled lower-resolution image from a higher-resolution image.
concepts.content:
In the Gaussian pyramid, each level loses some fine image details from the previous level. The Laplacian pyramid @Burt83 represents, at each level, what is present in a Gaussian pyramid image but not in the level below. This is calculated by expanding (upsampling) the lower-resolution Gaussian image to the same size as the higher-resolution image, then subtracting the two. This is done recursively.

To compute the Laplacian pyramid, we calculate the difference between $\mathbf{g}_k$ and $\mathbf{g}_{k+1}$. First, upsample $\mathbf{g}_{k+1}$ to the size of $\mathbf{g}_k$. Let $\mathbf{F}_k = \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{U}_k$ be the upsample-and-blur operator for level $k$, where $\mathbf{U}_k$ inserts zeros between samples and $\mathbf{B}_k$ is the same blur filter used in the Gaussian pyramid. The Laplacian pyramid coefficients at level $k$ are:
$$\mathbf{l}_k = \mathbf{g}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1} = (\mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{G}_k) \mathbf{g}_k = \mathbf{L}_k \mathbf{g}_k$$

One block of Laplacian pyramid computation is shown in the diagram.

@fig-laplacpyr shows the Laplacian pyramid for an image. To compute an $N$-level Laplacian pyramid, first compute a Gaussian pyramid with $N+1$ levels. The last Gaussian level is the low-pass residual.

The Laplacian pyramid is built independently for each color channel.

Matrix forms for 1D inputs and operators are given, showing the detailed computation. The factor 2 compensates for zero insertion reducing average signal value.

Interestingly, the Laplacian pyramid is an invertible transform.
concepts.motivation_md: The Laplacian pyramid captures image details lost between Gaussian pyramid levels, enabling efficient multiscale image representation and reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:

- It is computed by subtracting an upsampled, blurred lower-resolution image from a higher-resolution image.
- The Laplacian pyramid is invertible and built independently per color channel.

key_passage.text: The Laplacian pyramid is simple: it represents, at each level, what is present in a Gaussian pyramid image of one level, but not present at the level below it. We calculate that by expanding the lower-resolution Gaussian pyramid image to the same pixel resolution as the neighboring higher-resolution Gaussian pyramid image, then subtracting the two. This calculation is made in a recursive, telescoping fashion.

motivation.text: In the Gaussian pyramid, each level losses some of the fine image details available in the previous level.

example.text: Let's look at the steps for calculating a Laplacian pyramid. What we want is to compute the difference between \mathbf{g}_k and \mathbf{g}_{k+1}. To do this first we need to upsample the image \mathbf{g}_{k+1} so that it has the same size as \mathbf{g}_k. Let \mathbf{F}_k = \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{U}_k be the upsample-and-blur operator for pyramid level k. The operator \mathbf{F}_k applies first the upsampling operator \mathbf{U}_k, that inserts zeros between samples, followed by blurring by the same filter \mathbf{B}_k than the one we used for the Gaussian pyramid. The Laplacian pyramid coefficients, \mathbf{l}_k, at pyramid level k, are: $$\mathbf{l}_{k} = \mathbf{g}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1} = (\mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{G}_k) \mathbf{g}_{k} = \mathbf{L}_k \mathbf{g}_{k}$$ One **block** of the Laplacian pyramid computation.

concepts.title: low-pass residual
concepts.one_liner: The low-pass residual in the Laplacian pyramid enables recursive reconstruction of the Gaussian pyramid and original image.
concepts.content:
The low-pass residual signal associated with the Laplacian pyramid allows recursive reconstruction of the corresponding Gaussian pyramid. Recall that in the Gaussian pyramid, level 1 is the original image itself, so we can reconstruct the original image from the Laplacian pyramid.

Reconstruction is done recursively from $k = N-1$ down to $k=0$:
$$\mathbf{g}_k = \mathbf{l}_k + \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1}$$

The diagram in @fig-laplacian_pyr_architecture shows the Gaussian pyramid, the Laplacian pyramid, and the Laplacian inversion for a three-level Laplacian pyramid. Reconstruction uses the Laplacian pyramid coefficients $\mathbf{l}_0, \mathbf{l}_1, ..., \mathbf{l}_2$ and the low-pass residual $\mathbf{g}_3$ to recover the input signal $\boldsymbol\ell = \mathbf{g}_0$.

concepts.recap_md:
- The low-pass residual enables recursive reconstruction of the Gaussian pyramid.
- Reconstruction uses Laplacian pyramid coefficients and the low-pass residual.
- This process recovers the original image from the Laplacian pyramid.

concepts.title: steerable filter bank

concepts.content:
We analyze orientation using a steerable filter bank, shown in @fig-steerable_pyr_sp3Filters. We form a decomposition in scale by introducing a low-pass filter designed to work with the selected bandpass filters, and recursively break the low-pass filtered component into angular and low-pass frequency components. Pyramid subsampling steps are preceded by sufficient low-pass filtering to remove aliasing.

concepts.title: steerable pyramid architecture
concepts.one_liner: The architecture has two parts: (1) the analysis network (or encoder) that transforms the input image $x$ into a representation composed of subbands and the low pass residual; and (2) the synthesis network (or decoder) that reconstructs the input from the representation.
concepts.content:
The following block diagram (@fig-steerable_pyr_architecture) shows the steps to build a two-level steerable pyramid and the reconstruction of the input. The architecture has two parts: (1) the analysis network (or encoder) that transforms the input image $x$ into a representation composed of
$r=\left[ b_{0,0},...,b_{0,n}, b_{1,0},...b_{1,n},...,b_{k-1,0},...b_{k-1,n} \right]$
and the low pass residual $g_{k-1}$; and (2) the synthesis network (or decoder) that reconstructs the input from the representation $r$.

(see figure: Steerable pyramid architecture.)

@fig-steerable_pyr_clock shows an example of an image and its steerable pyramid decomposition using four orientations and three scales. The steerable pyramid is a self-inverting overcomplete representation (more coefficients than pixels).

(see figure: Steerable pyramid representation (three levels and four orientations). Why is that each orientation subband seems to indicate a different time?)

concepts.recap_md:
- The steerable pyramid architecture has an analysis (encoder) and synthesis (decoder) network.
- The encoder produces oriented subbands and a low-pass residual.
- The representation is overcomplete and allows perfect reconstruction.

concepts.title: A Pictorial Summary
concepts.one_liner: @fig-pictorialsummary_pyr shows a pictorial summary of the different pyramid representations we've discussed in this chapter, illustrating projection matrices for 1D and 2D cases.
concepts.content:
## A Pictorial Summary

@fig-pictorialsummary_pyr shows a pictorial summary of the different pyramid representations we've discussed in this chapter. The figure shows the projection matrices $\mathbf{P}$ for each transformation, both in the 1D case and 2D case. Each projection matrix is formed by stacking the projection matrices of each pyramid level.

@fig-pictorialsummary_pyr (a-c) start with a 1D input signal of length 16. For instance, for a three-level Gaussian pyramid, @fig-pictorialsummary_pyr (b) shows the following projection matrix:
$$\mathbf{P} =  
    \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{I} \\
    \mathbf{G}_0 \\
    \mathbf{G}_1 \\
    \end{bmatrix}$$ The first block is the identity matrix as the first level is the input image itself.

For a two-level Laplacian pyramid with a Gaussian residual, the projection matrix $\mathbf{P}$ is (@fig-pictorialsummary_pyr[b]):
$$\mathbf{P} =  
    \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{L}_0 \\
    \mathbf{L}_1 \\
    \mathbf{G}_1 \\
    \end{bmatrix}$$

The Fourier transform gives a complex-valued output (represented in color) and is global, that is, each output coefficient depends, in general, on every input pixel. The Gaussian pyramid is seen to be banded, showing that it is a localized transform where the output values only depend on pixels in a neighborhood. It is an overcomplete representation, shown by the transform matrix being taller than it is wide. The Laplacian pyramid is a band-passed image representation, except for the low-pass residual layer, shown in the bottom rows. For this matrix, zero is plotted as gray.

Figures @fig-pictorialsummary_pyr (d-h) show the projection matrices when the input is a 2D image of size 16×16 pixels. First, the image is represented as a column vector of length 256=16×16 values. @fig-pictorialsummary_pyr (d) shows the projection matrix of the 2D Fourier transform, a square matrix of size 256×256, composed of small blocks of size 16×16 that look like 1D Fourier transforms. Figures @fig-pictorialsummary_pyr (e and f) show the Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids, respectively.

Figures @fig-pictorialsummary_pyr (g-h) show the steerable pyramid representation, depending on the number of orientations (@fig-pictorialsummary_pyr g is a pyramid with two orientations and @fig-pictorialsummary_pyr h has four orientations per scale). The steerable pyramid representation can be very overcomplete (the matrix is much taller than wide).

The steerable pyramid is an overcomplete, multiorientation representation. We only show the steerable pyramid for 2D images as in 1D, image orientation isn't defined. The multiple orientations, and non-aliased subbands cause the representation to be very overcomplete, much taller than it is wide. The last block of the steerable pyramid projection matrices computes the low-pass residual.

(see figure: Visual comparison of linear transform image representations discussed in this chapter. All the transforms are visualized as a matrix where the number of rows is the size of the input, and the number...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding different pyramid representations and their projection matrices helps visualize how image transforms localize information in scale, orientation, and frequency domains.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pyramid representations can be visualized as projection matrices stacking each level.
- Gaussian pyramids are localized and overcomplete; Laplacian pyramids are band-passed.
- Steerable pyramids add orientation, are highly overcomplete, and compute low-pass residuals.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform reveals spatial frequency content but lacks spatial localization; Gaussian, Laplacian, and steerable pyramids provide multiscale and orientation representations with varying completeness and applications.
concepts.content:
## Concluding Remarks

To recap briefly, the Fourier transform reveals spatial frequency content of the image wonderfully, but suffers from having no spatial localization. A Gaussian pyramid provides a multiscale representation of the image, useful for applying a fixed-scale algorithm to an image over a range of spatial scales. But it doesn't break the image into finer components than simply a range of low-pass filtered versions. The representation is overcomplete; that is, there are more pixels in the Gaussian pyramid representation of an image than there are in the image itself.

The Laplacian pyramid reveals what is captured at one spatial scale of a Gaussian pyramid, and not seen at the lower-resolution level above it. Like the Gaussian pyramid, it is overcomplete. It is useful for various image manipulation tasks, allowing you to treat different spatial frequency bands separately.

The steerable pyramid adds orientation information into the representation, and the representation can be very overcomplete (the matrix is much taller than wide). The steerable pyramid has negligible aliasing artifacts and so can be useful for various image analysis applications.

In image processing applications (i.e., image compression, denoising, etc.) people have used other transforms. For instance, the Haar/wavelet/QMF pyramid @Adelson87b brings in some limited orientation analysis and different than the other pyramid representations, is complete rather than overcomplete. This helps it for image compression applications, but hurts it for others because each subband depends on information in other subbands to let it reconstruct the original image without artifacts. So if you alter one band without altering the corresponding other ones, you can easily introduce artifacts (although artifacts will also appear in overcompleted representations).

Another important framework for multiscale image analysis, not presented in this book, is **scale space**. For an in-depth presentation of this topic, we direct the reader to @Lindeberg1994.
concepts.motivation_md: Different image representations balance spatial localization, frequency decomposition, orientation, and completeness, enabling varied applications like compression, denoising, and analysis.

- Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids provide multiscale, overcomplete image representations.
- Steerable pyramids add orientation and reduce aliasing, useful for analysis.
